deep.reconstruction:
The page has two columns: right column first, left column second. It gives the quadratic (Landen–Gauss) transformation of the first-kind elliptic integral in two notations. The trigonometric version is the invariance of the integral under the arithmetic-geometric-mean step (a,b) -> ((a+b)/2, sqrt(ab)). In what follows, k = mu, k' = sqrt(1-mu^2) and lambda = (1-k')/(1+k'). Gauss writes the differential as ∂x.

(1) Algebraic form. The claim is
∫ dx/sqrt((1-x^2)(1-k^2 x^2)) = ∫ dy / [ ((1+k')/2) sqrt((1-y^2)(1-lambda^2 y^2)) ].
The substitution is 1/x = ((1-k')/2) y + ((1+k')/2)(1/y), i.e. x = 2y/((1+k') + (1-k') y^2).

Implicit steps (mine):
- 1+lambda = 2/(1+k') and 2 sqrt(lambda)/(1+lambda) = k.
- The substitution is therefore x = (1+lambda) y/(1+lambda y^2). This is the Gauss/Landen transformation sn((1+lambda)v, k) = (1+lambda) sn(v,lambda)/(1+lambda sn^2(v,lambda)).
- It gives dx/sqrt((1-x^2)(1-k^2x^2)) = (1+lambda) dy/sqrt((1-y^2)(1-lambda^2y^2)).
- Since 1+lambda = 2/(1+k'), this is exactly Gauss's factor 1/((1+k')/2).

(2) Trigonometric form. Put x = sin phi and y = sin psi:
∫ dphi/sqrt(1-mu^2 sin^2 phi) = ∫ dpsi / [ ((1+k')/2) sqrt(1-lambda^2 sin^2 psi) ].

(3) Gauss then sets mu^2 = (a^2-b^2)/a^2, so that k' = b/a (the 'b/a' written beside the formula). With a' = (a+b)/2 this gives:
- (1+k')/2 = a'/a;
- lambda = (a-b)/(a+b);
- a^2 cos^2 phi + b^2 sin^2 phi = a^2 (1-mu^2 sin^2 phi).
Hence
∫ a dphi/sqrt(a^2cos^2phi + b^2 sin^2phi) = ∫ a dpsi/( a' sqrt(1-((a-b)/(a+b))^2 sin^2 psi) ).

(4) Writing 1 - lambda^2 sin^2 psi = cos^2 psi + (1-lambda^2) sin^2 psi, and noting 1-lambda^2 = 4ab/(a+b)^2 = b'^2/a'^2 with b' = sqrt(ab), the right side becomes
∫ a dpsi/( a' sqrt(cos^2psi + (b'^2/a'^2) sin^2psi) ).

(5) Dividing by a and renaming psi -> phi' gives the AGM invariance:
∫ dphi/sqrt(a^2cos^2phi + b^2 sin^2phi) = ∫ dphi'/sqrt(a'^2cos^2phi' + b'^2 sin^2phi'),
with the substitution 1/sin phi = ((a+b)/(2a)) (1/sin phi') + ((a-b)/(2a)) sin phi'.
Equivalently, sin phi = 2a sin phi'/((a+b) + (a-b) sin^2 phi').

As phi' runs over 0..pi/2, phi also runs over 0..pi/2. So the complete integrals over a quarter period are equal. Iterating the step makes the complete integral equal to pi/(2 M(a,b)), where M is the arithmetic-geometric mean.

This is the central lemma of Gauss's AGM theory of elliptic integrals. The page's neighbours (theta-series computations 'zur 7 Theilung' on the next page; astronomical observations on the previous one) are consistent with his work on the AGM and lemniscatic/elliptic functions.
errors: No mathematical errors found; all steps check out.
Minor notational point: in the first displayed formula the factor (1+sqrt(1-mu mu))/2 multiplies the radical in the denominator. Read that way, the formula is correct.

results.what: Quadratic transformation of the first-kind elliptic integral via 1/x = ((1-k')/2) y + ((1+k')/2)/y, with new modulus lambda = (1-k')/(1+k') and multiplier 2/(1+k').
results.modern_name: Landen's transformation (descending), in Gauss's form (Gauss transformation)
results.usually_credited_to: John Landen (1775); Lagrange (1784); Gauss (1799 diary, published 1818); Legendre

results.what: Invariance of ∫ dphi/sqrt(a^2cos^2phi + b^2sin^2phi) under (a,b) -> ((a+b)/2, sqrt(ab)) with substitution 1/sin phi = ((a+b)/2a)/sin phi' + ((a-b)/2a) sin phi'.
results.modern_name: Arithmetic-geometric mean invariance of the complete elliptic integral (K = pi/(2 AGM))
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (diary 1799; published in 'Determinatio attractionis...', 1818), building on Lagrange

deep.surprise_reason: This is Gauss's well-known AGM transformation. The substitution is essentially identical to the one he published in 1818 (sin T = 2m sin T'/((m+n)+(m-n)sin^2 T')), and it is documented in the Nachlass (Werke III). It is a clean working draft of known material.

1 - lambda^2 = b'^2/a'^2 with a' = (a+b)/2, b' = sqrt(ab); should be 0.

transcription_corrections: Gauss's '∂x', '∂y', '∂φ', '∂ψ' denote ordinary differentials dx, dy, dφ, dψ.
The isolated 'b/a' after 'μμ = (aa-bb)/aa' is a marginal note meaning sqrt(1-μμ) = b/a. It is not part of an equation.
In the first line the factor (1+sqrt(1-μμ))/2 belongs to the denominator of the right-hand integrand, multiplying the radical.
Last line reads: 1/sinφ = (a+b)/(2a) · 1/sinφ' + (a-b)/(2a) · sinφ'. This is correct as transcribed.
